title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Wages and Profit in the Different Employments of Labour and Stock

Within the same neighbourhood, the total package of advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock must either be perfectly equal or constantly moving toward equality. If one employment in a given area were clearly more advantageous than the rest, so many people would pour into it that its advantages would quickly fall back to the level of the others; and if one were clearly less advantageous, so many would abandon it that the same levelling would happen in reverse. At least this is what would occur in a society where things were left to follow their natural course, where there was perfect liberty, and where everyone was free both to choose whatever occupation he thought suitable and to change it whenever he pleased. Each person's own interest would drive him toward the advantageous employment and away from the disadvantageous one.

In fact, money wages and profits differ enormously across Europe from one employment of labour and stock to another. But this difference comes from two sources. Part of it arises from features of the employments themselves, which, either in reality or at least in people's imaginations, make up for a small money gain in some and offset a large one in others. The rest arises from the policies of Europe, which nowhere leave matters at perfect liberty.
Examining those features and those policies separately divides this chapter into two parts.
Part I: Inequalities arising from the nature of the employments themselves.

As far as I have been able to observe, there are five main features that make up for a small money gain in some employments and offset a large one in others. First, how pleasant or unpleasant the work itself is. Second, how easy and cheap, or how difficult and expensive, the work is to learn. Third, how steady or irregular the employment is. Fourth, how much or how little trust must be placed in those who do it. And fifth, how likely or unlikely a person is to succeed at it.

First, wages vary with how easy or hard the work is, how clean or dirty, and how honourable or dishonourable. In most places, taking the year as a whole, a journeyman tailor earns less than a journeyman weaver, because his work is much easier. A journeyman weaver earns less than a journeyman smith, because, although the work is not always easier, it is much cleaner. A journeyman blacksmith, though a skilled craftsman, seldom earns as much in twelve hours as a collier, who is only a labourer, earns in eight; the collier's work is dirtier, more dangerous, and carried on in daylight above ground. Honour makes up a large part of the reward in every honourable profession, which, in pure money terms and all things considered, are generally underpaid, as I shall try to show later. Disgrace works the opposite way. Butchering is a brutal and hateful trade, yet in most places it is more profitable than most ordinary trades. The most detestable employment of all, that of public executioner, is, relative to the amount of work done, better paid than any ordinary trade whatever.

Hunting and fishing, the most important occupations of mankind in the primitive state of society, become its most pleasant pastimes in its advanced state, and people now pursue for enjoyment what they once did out of necessity. In an advanced society, therefore, anyone who follows as a trade what others pursue as a hobby is always very poor. Fishermen have been poor since the days of Theocritus (see Idyll xxi). A poacher is everywhere a very poor man in Great Britain, and in countries where the strictness of the law allows no poachers, the licensed hunter is hardly better off. The natural attraction of these activities draws more people into them than can live comfortably by them, so the product of their labour, relative to its quantity, always reaches the market too cheaply to give the workers anything more than the barest subsistence.

Unpleasantness and disgrace affect the profits of stock just as they affect wages. The keeper of an inn or tavern, who is never master of his own house and is exposed to the rudeness of every drunkard, runs neither a very pleasant nor a very respectable business; yet there is scarcely any ordinary trade in which a small amount of stock yields so large a profit.
Second, wages vary with how easy and cheap, or how difficult and expensive, the trade is to learn.

When an expensive machine is built, we expect that the extra work it performs before it wears out will repay the capital spent on it, along with at least the ordinary profits. A person trained for an occupation that demands extraordinary skill and dexterity, at the cost of much labour and time, is like one of these expensive machines. We expect that the work he learns to do will, over and above the usual wages of common labour, repay him the whole cost of his education plus at least the ordinary profits on an equally valuable capital. And it must do this within a reasonable time, given the very uncertain length of human life, just as the machine must do so within its more predictable lifespan.
This principle is what underlies the difference between the wages of skilled labour and those of common labour.

European policy treats the work of all mechanics, craftsmen, and manufacturers as skilled labour, and that of all country labourers as common labour. It assumes the former is more refined and delicate than the latter. In some cases that may be true, but in most it is quite the reverse, as I shall try to show later. To qualify a person for the skilled kind of work, the laws and customs of Europe therefore require an apprenticeship, though enforced with varying strictness from place to place; the other kind they leave open to everyone. Throughout the apprenticeship, all of the apprentice's labour belongs to his master. Meanwhile the apprentice must in many cases be supported by his parents or relatives, and in almost all cases be clothed by them. Money is also commonly paid to the master for teaching the trade, and those who cannot pay give time instead, binding themselves for more than the usual number of years; this is always a loss to the apprentice, even though, because apprentices are usually idle, it is not always a gain to the master. In country labour, by contrast, the labourer learns the harder parts of his work while doing the easier parts, and his own labour supports him through every stage of his employment. It is reasonable, then, that in Europe the wages of mechanics, craftsmen, and manufacturers should be somewhat higher than those of common labourers, and they are; their higher earnings make them be regarded in most places as a superior rank of people. This superiority, however, is generally very small. The daily or weekly earnings of journeymen in the more ordinary kinds of manufacture, such as plain linen and woollen cloth, work out on average, in most places, to very little more than the daily wages of common labourers. Their work is, admittedly, steadier and more uniform, and over the whole year their advantage in earnings may be somewhat greater. Even so, it appears to be no more than enough to make up for the greater cost of their training. Education in the ingenious arts and in the liberal professions is more time-consuming and more expensive still, so the money rewards of painters and sculptors, of lawyers and physicians, ought to be much more generous, and they are.

The profits of stock seem barely affected by how easy or hard the trade is to learn. All the various ways stock is commonly employed in large towns seem in fact almost equally easy and equally hard to master. One branch of foreign or domestic trade cannot be much more complicated than another.
Third, wages in different occupations vary with how steady or irregular the employment is.

Some trades offer far steadier employment than others. In most manufactures a journeyman can be fairly certain of work on almost every day of the year that he is fit to work. A mason or bricklayer, by contrast, can work neither in hard frost nor in foul weather, and at all other times his work depends on the occasional demands of his customers, so he is frequently left with nothing to do. What he earns while employed must therefore not only support him while idle but also compensate him somewhat for the anxious, despairing moments that thinking about so precarious a situation must sometimes bring. Accordingly, where the reckoned earnings of most manufacturers are roughly on a level with the daily wages of common labourers, those of masons and bricklayers generally run from one and a half to twice those wages. Where common labourers earn four or five shillings a week, masons and bricklayers often earn seven or eight; where the former earn six, the latter often earn nine or ten; and where the former earn nine or ten, as in London, the latter commonly earn fifteen or eighteen. Yet no kind of skilled labour seems easier to learn than that of masons and bricklayers. In London, chairmen are said to work sometimes as bricklayers during the summer. The high wages of these workmen, then, are not so much the reward of their skill as compensation for the irregularity of their employment.

A house-carpenter seems to practise a somewhat more refined and ingenious trade than a mason, yet in most places, though not everywhere, his daily wages are somewhat lower. His work, though heavily dependent on his customers' occasional demands, does not depend on them so completely, and it is not interrupted by the weather.

When trades that normally provide steady work happen not to do so in a particular place, the workmen's wages always rise well above their usual ratio to common labour. In London, almost all journeymen craftsmen are liable to be hired and dismissed by their masters from day to day and week to week, just as day-labourers are elsewhere. So even the lowest order of craftsmen, journeymen tailors, earn their half-crown a day, though eighteen pence may be taken as the wage of common labour. In small towns and country villages, the wages of journeymen tailors often barely equal those of common labour, but in London they are frequently out of work for many weeks, especially in summer.

When irregular employment is combined with hard, unpleasant, and dirty work, it sometimes pushes the wages of the most common labour above those of the most skilful craftsmen. A collier working by the piece is reckoned at Newcastle to earn commonly about double, and in many parts of Scotland about triple, the wages of common labour. His high wages arise entirely from the hardship, unpleasantness, and dirtiness of his work; his employment, in most cases, can be as steady as he chooses. The coal-heavers in London do work that almost matches that of colliers in hardship, dirtiness, and unpleasantness, and, because of the unavoidable irregularity in when coal-ships arrive, the work of most of them is necessarily very irregular. If colliers commonly earn double and triple the wages of common labour, then, it should not seem unreasonable that coal-heavers should sometimes earn four or five times those wages. In an inquiry made into their condition a few years ago, it was found that, at the rates they were then paid, they could earn from six to ten shillings a day. Six shillings is about four times the wages of common labour in London, and in every particular trade the lowest ordinary earnings may always be taken as those of the great majority. However extravagant those earnings may look, if they were more than enough to compensate for all the disagreeable features of the work, so many competitors would soon appear that, in a trade with no exclusive privilege, they would quickly be driven down to a lower rate.
How steady or irregular employment is cannot affect the ordinary profits of stock in any particular trade. Whether the stock is kept constantly at work depends not on the trade but on the trader.
Fourth, wages vary with how little or how much trust must be placed in the workmen.

The wages of goldsmiths and jewellers are everywhere higher than those of many other workers of equal, or even far greater, ingenuity, because of the precious materials placed in their care. We trust our health to the physician, and our fortune, and sometimes our life and reputation, to the lawyer and attorney. Such confidence could not safely be placed in people of very low or humble standing. Their reward must therefore be enough to give them the position in society that so important a trust requires. The long time and great expense that must go into their education, combined with this need for standing, necessarily raise the price of their labour still further.

When a person trades only with his own stock, no trust is involved; and the credit others extend to him depends not on the nature of the trade but on their opinion of his wealth, honesty, and prudence. The different rates of profit in different branches of trade cannot, therefore, arise from different degrees of trust placed in the traders.
Fifth, wages in different employments vary with how likely or unlikely success in them is.

The chance that a given person will ever become qualified for the occupation he is trained for varies greatly from one occupation to another. In most mechanical trades success is almost certain, but in the liberal professions it is very uncertain. Apprentice your son to a shoemaker, and there is little doubt he will learn to make a pair of shoes; but send him to study law, and it is at least twenty to one that he will ever become skilled enough to make a living at it. In a perfectly fair lottery, those who draw the prizes ought to win everything lost by those who draw blanks. In a profession where twenty fail for every one who succeeds, that one ought to gain everything the unsuccessful twenty would have gained. The barrister who perhaps, at nearly forty years of age, begins to make something from his profession, ought to receive payment not only for his own long and costly education but for that of more than twenty others who will likely never earn anything from it. However extravagant the fees of barristers may sometimes appear, their real return never amounts to this. Work out, for any particular place, what all the workers in an ordinary trade such as shoemaking or weaving are likely to earn in a year and what they are likely to spend, and you will generally find earnings exceeding spending. But make the same calculation for all the barristers and law students in all the various Inns of Court, and you will find that their yearly earnings are only a very small fraction of their yearly expenses, even if you rate earnings as high and expenses as low as you reasonably can. The lottery of the law, then, is far from a perfectly fair one; and law, like many other liberal and honourable professions, is plainly underpaid in money terms.

These professions nevertheless hold their own against other occupations, and despite these discouragements all the most generous and high-minded spirits are eager to crowd into them. Two different causes make them attractive. First, the desire for the reputation that comes with outstanding excellence in any of them; and second, the natural confidence that everyone has, more or less, not only in his own abilities but in his own good luck.

To excel in a profession in which few even reach an ordinary standard is the surest sign of what we call genius, or superior talent. The public admiration that follows such distinguished ability always forms part of its reward, larger or smaller in proportion to how high the ability is. It makes up a considerable part of the reward in medicine, a still greater part perhaps in law, and in poetry and philosophy almost the whole of it.

There are certain very pleasing and beautiful talents whose possession commands a kind of admiration, but whose exercise for money is regarded, whether reasonably or out of prejudice, as a sort of public prostitution. The money reward of those who use such talents in this way must therefore be enough to pay not only for the time, labour, and expense of acquiring them but also for the discredit attached to making a living by them. The extravagant rewards of actors, opera-singers, opera-dancers, and the like rest on these two principles: the rarity and beauty of the talents, and the discredit of using them in this way. It seems absurd at first that we should look down on the people while rewarding their talents with the most lavish generosity, yet in doing the one we are necessarily forced to do the other. Should public opinion or prejudice ever change toward such occupations, their money rewards would quickly shrink, because more people would take them up and competition would soon drive down the price of their labour. Such talents, though far from common, are by no means as rare as people imagine. Many possess them in great perfection but scorn to use them this way, and many more could acquire them if anything honourable could be earned by them.

The excessive conceit that most people have about their own abilities is an old failing remarked on by philosophers and moralists of every age. Their absurd over-confidence in their own good luck has been noticed less, yet it is, if anything, even more universal. There is no one alive who, in reasonable health and spirits, does not have some share of it. Every man more or less overvalues the chance of gain, and most men undervalue the chance of loss; hardly anyone in reasonable health and spirits values the chance of loss at more than it is really worth.

That the chance of gain is naturally overvalued, we can see from the universal success of lotteries. The world has never seen, and never will see, a perfectly fair lottery, one in which the total winnings equal the total losses, because the organizer must make something from it. In state lotteries the tickets are really worth less than the price paid by the original subscribers, yet they commonly sell on the market at twenty, thirty, and sometimes forty per cent above that price. The vain hope of winning one of the big prizes is the sole cause of this demand. Even the soberest people scarcely regard it as folly to pay a small sum for the chance of winning ten or twenty thousand pounds, though they know that even that small sum is perhaps twenty or thirty per cent more than the chance is worth. In a lottery where no prize exceeded twenty pounds, even though it would otherwise come much nearer to a perfectly fair one than the usual state lotteries, there would not be the same demand for tickets. To improve their chance at the big prizes, some people buy several tickets, and others buy small shares in a still greater number. Yet there is no surer proposition in mathematics than that the more tickets you take on, the more likely you are to lose. Take on every ticket in the lottery and you lose for certain; the more tickets you hold, the closer you come to this certainty.

That the chance of loss is frequently undervalued, and almost never valued at more than it is worth, we can learn from the very modest profits of insurers. For insurance against fire or sea-risk to be a viable business at all, the usual premium must be enough to cover the usual losses, pay the cost of management, and yield the same profit that an equal capital would have earned in any ordinary trade. The person who pays no more than this clearly pays no more than the real value of the risk, the lowest price at which he can reasonably expect to be insured. Yet although many people have made a little money from insurance, very few have made a great fortune; and from this alone it seems clear enough that the ordinary balance of profit and loss is no more favourable here than in other ordinary trades by which so many people grow rich. Modest as the insurance premium usually is, many people despise the risk too much to bother paying it. Taking the whole kingdom on average, nineteen houses in twenty, or rather perhaps ninety-nine in a hundred, are not insured against fire. Sea-risk alarms most people more, so the proportion of ships insured to those uninsured is much greater; yet many still sail in all seasons, and even in wartime, with no insurance. Sometimes this may be done without imprudence: when a great company, or even a great merchant, has twenty or thirty ships at sea, they can, in effect, insure one another, and the premiums saved on all of them may more than cover the losses they are likely to meet in the ordinary run of chances. In most cases, however, neglecting to insure ships, like neglecting to insure houses, results not from any such careful calculation but from sheer thoughtless rashness and a presumptuous contempt for the risk.

Contempt for risk and a presumptuous hope of success are never more active than at the age when young people choose their professions. How little the fear of misfortune can then balance the hope of good luck appears even more plainly in the eagerness of ordinary people to enlist as soldiers or go to sea than in the eagerness of those of better standing to enter the so-called liberal professions.

What a common soldier stands to lose is obvious enough. Disregarding the danger, however, young volunteers never enlist so readily as at the start of a new war; and though they have scarcely any chance of promotion, they picture to themselves, in their youthful fancies, a thousand occasions for winning honour and distinction that never come. These romantic hopes are the whole price of their blood. Their pay is less than that of common labourers, and in actual service their hardships are far greater.

The lottery of the sea is not quite so unfavourable as that of the army. The son of a respectable labourer or craftsman may often go to sea with his father's consent, but if he enlists as a soldier he always does so without it. Others see some chance of his making something by the one trade, while no one but himself sees any chance of his making anything by the other. The great admiral is less an object of public admiration than the great general, and the highest success at sea promises a less brilliant fortune and reputation than equal success on land. The same difference runs through all the lower ranks of promotion in both services. By the rules of precedence a captain in the navy ranks with a colonel in the army, but he does not rank with him in common opinion. Since the great prizes in this lottery are smaller, the smaller ones must be more numerous: common sailors, therefore, more often gain some fortune and promotion than common soldiers do, and it is the hope of those prizes that chiefly recommends the trade. Although their skill and dexterity are far superior to that of almost any craftsman, and although their whole life is one continual scene of hardship and danger, yet for all this skill and dexterity, and for all those hardships and dangers, so long as they remain common sailors they receive scarcely any reward beyond the pleasure of exercising the one and overcoming the other. Their wages are no greater than those of common labourers at the port that sets the rate for seamen's wages. Because they are continually moving from port to port, the monthly pay of those who sail from all the different ports of Great Britain is more nearly equal than that of any other workmen in those various places, and the rate at the port to and from which the greatest number sail, namely London, governs that of all the rest. In London the wages of most classes of workmen are about double those of the same classes in Edinburgh, yet the sailors who sail from London seldom earn more than three or four shillings a month above those who sail from Leith, and often the difference is not even that great. In peacetime, in the merchant service, the London rate runs from a guinea to about twenty-seven shillings a calendar month. A common labourer in London, at nine or ten shillings a week, may earn forty to forty-five shillings in a calendar month. The sailor, it is true, is supplied with provisions on top of his pay; but their value may not always exceed the difference between his pay and the labourer's, and even when it does, the excess is no clear gain to the sailor, because he cannot share it with the wife and family he must support out of his wages at home.

The dangers and narrow escapes of an adventurous life, far from discouraging young people, often seem to recommend a trade to them. A tender mother among the lower ranks is often afraid to send her son to school in a seaport town, in case the sight of the ships and the conversation and adventures of the sailors should tempt him to go to sea. The distant prospect of dangers from which we hope to escape by our own courage and skill is not unpleasant to us, and it does not raise wages in any employment. It is otherwise with dangers against which courage and skill are useless. In trades known to be very unhealthy, wages are always strikingly high. Unhealthiness is a kind of unpleasantness, and its effect on wages falls under that general heading.

In all the different employments of stock, the ordinary rate of profit varies more or less with the certainty or uncertainty of the returns. These are generally less uncertain in inland trade than in foreign trade, and less uncertain in some branches of foreign trade than in others: in the trade to North America, for example, than in the trade to Jamaica. The ordinary rate of profit always rises somewhat with the risk, but it does not seem to rise in proportion to it, or enough to compensate for it fully. Bankruptcies are most frequent in the riskiest trades. The riskiest of all, smuggling, though it is the most profitable when the venture succeeds, is the surest road to bankruptcy. The presumptuous hope of success seems to operate here as on every other occasion, luring so many adventurers into these hazardous trades that their competition drives profit below the level needed to compensate for the risk. To compensate for it fully, the usual returns ought, over and above the ordinary profits of stock, not only to cover all occasional losses but to yield the adventurers a surplus profit of the same kind as the profit of insurers. But if the usual returns were enough for all this, bankruptcies would be no more frequent in these trades than in others.

Of the five circumstances, then, that vary wages, only two affect the profits of stock: how pleasant or unpleasant the business is, and how risky or secure it is. In pleasantness or unpleasantness there is little or no difference among the great majority of the different employments of stock, though there is a great deal among the different employments of labour; and the ordinary profit of stock, though it rises with risk, does not always seem to rise in proportion to it. It should follow from all this that, within the same society or neighbourhood, the average ordinary rates of profit in the different employments of stock should be more nearly equal than the money wages of the different kinds of labour.

And so they are. The difference between the earnings of a common labourer and those of a well-employed lawyer or physician is obviously much greater than the difference between the ordinary profits of any two branches of trade. Besides, the apparent difference in the profits of different trades is usually a deception arising from our failure to distinguish what ought to be counted as wages from what ought to be counted as profit.

An apothecary's profit has become a byword for something uncommonly extravagant. Yet this great apparent profit is often no more than the reasonable wages of labour. An apothecary's skill is a far more refined and delicate matter than that of any other craftsman, and the trust placed in him is far more important: he is the physician of the poor in every case, and of the rich whenever the distress or danger is not very great. His reward, then, ought to match his skill and his trust, and it generally comes from the price at which he sells his drugs. But all the drugs the best-employed apothecary in a large market town sells in a year may not cost him more than thirty or forty pounds. Even if he sells them for three or four hundred, that is, at a thousand per cent profit, this may often be no more than the reasonable wages of his labour, charged in the only way he can charge them, namely on the price of his drugs. Most of the apparent profit is really wages disguised in the dress of profit.

In a small seaport town a little grocer will make forty or fifty per cent on a stock of a single hundred pounds, while a considerable wholesale merchant in the same place will scarcely make eight or ten per cent on a stock of ten thousand. The grocer's trade may be necessary for the convenience of the inhabitants, and the small size of the market may not allow a larger capital to be employed in it. Still, the grocer must not only live by his trade but live by it in keeping with the qualifications it requires. Besides having a little capital, he must be able to read, write, and keep accounts, and must be a tolerable judge of perhaps fifty or sixty different kinds of goods, their prices, qualities, and the markets where they can be had cheapest. In short, he must have all the knowledge a great merchant needs, lacking only the larger capital to become one. Thirty or forty pounds a year cannot be considered too great a reward for the labour of so accomplished a person. Deduct this from the seemingly great profits of his capital, and little more will remain, perhaps, than the ordinary profits of stock. Here too, most of the apparent profit is really wages.

The difference between the apparent profit of retail and that of wholesale trade is much smaller in the capital than in small towns and country villages. Where ten thousand pounds can be employed in the grocery trade, the wages of the grocer's labour add only a trifling amount to the real profits of so large a stock; the apparent profits of the wealthy retailer are therefore much nearer those of the wholesale merchant. For this reason goods sold by retail are generally as cheap, and often much cheaper, in the capital than in small towns and country villages. Grocery goods, for example, are generally much cheaper, and bread and butchers' meat are often as cheap. It costs no more to bring grocery goods to the great town than to the country village, but it costs much more to bring corn and cattle, since most of them must be brought from a much greater distance. Since the prime cost of grocery goods is the same in both places, they are cheapest where the smallest profit is charged on them. The prime cost of bread and butchers' meat is greater in the great town than in the country village; so although the profit is less, they are not always cheaper there but often equally cheap. In articles like bread and butchers' meat, the same cause that lowers apparent profit raises prime cost. By giving employment to larger stocks, the size of the market lowers apparent profit; but by requiring supplies from a greater distance, it raises prime cost. This fall in the one and rise in the other seem in most cases nearly to cancel each other out, which is probably why, though the prices of corn and cattle commonly differ greatly across the kingdom, the prices of bread and butchers' meat are generally very nearly the same throughout most of it.

Although the profits of stock, in both wholesale and retail trade, are generally lower in the capital than in small towns and country villages, great fortunes are often built from small beginnings in the former and almost never in the latter. In small towns and country villages, because the market is narrow, trade cannot always be expanded as stock expands. In such places, therefore, though one person's rate of profit may be very high, the total amount of his profits can never be very great, and neither, consequently, can his yearly accumulation. In great towns, on the contrary, trade can be expanded as stock grows, and the credit of a frugal and prospering man grows much faster than his stock. His trade expands in proportion to both, the total of his profits is proportional to the extent of his trade, and his yearly accumulation is proportional to the total of his profits. It seldom happens, however, even in great towns, that great fortunes are made in any one regular, established, well-known branch of business, but rather through a long life of industry, frugality, and attention. Sudden fortunes are indeed sometimes made in such places by what is called speculation. The speculative merchant carries on no one regular, established, or well-known branch of business: he is a corn merchant this year, a wine merchant the next, and a sugar, tobacco, or tea merchant the year after. He enters any trade when he foresees that it is likely to be unusually profitable, and quits it when he foresees that its profits are likely to fall back to the level of other trades. His profits and losses, therefore, can bear no regular proportion to those of any one established and well-known branch of business. A bold adventurer may sometimes win a considerable fortune by two or three successful speculations, but he is just as likely to lose one by two or three unsuccessful ones. This trade can be carried on nowhere but in great towns; only in places of the most extensive commerce and correspondence can the intelligence it requires be had.

The five circumstances mentioned above, though they cause considerable inequalities in wages and profits, cause none in the total of the advantages and disadvantages, real or imagined, of the different employments of either labour or stock. Their very nature is such that they make up for a small money gain in some and offset a large one in others.

For this equality in the whole of their advantages and disadvantages to hold, however, three things are required, even where there is the most perfect freedom. First, the employments must be well known and long established in the neighbourhood. Second, they must be in their ordinary, or what we may call their natural, state. And third, they must be the sole or principal employments of those who occupy them.
First, this equality can hold only in employments that are well known and have long been established in the neighbourhood.

All other things being equal, wages are generally higher in new trades than in old ones. When a projector tries to set up a new manufacture, he must at first entice his workmen away from other employments with higher wages than they could earn in their own trades, or than the nature of his work would otherwise require; and a considerable time must pass before he dares to reduce them to the common level. Manufactures whose demand depends entirely on fashion and fancy are constantly changing and seldom last long enough to count as old established manufactures, while those whose demand depends chiefly on use or necessity change less, and the same form or fabric may stay in demand for whole centuries. Wages, therefore, are likely to be higher in the first kind of manufacture than in the second. Birmingham deals chiefly in manufactures of the first kind, Sheffield in those of the second, and the wages of labour in those two places are said to match this difference in the nature of their manufactures.

Setting up any new manufacture, any new branch of commerce, or any new practice in agriculture is always a speculation from which the projector promises himself extraordinary profits. These profits are sometimes very great and sometimes, perhaps more often, quite the opposite; but in general they bear no regular proportion to those of other old trades in the neighbourhood. If the project succeeds, they are commonly very high at first; and once the trade or practice becomes thoroughly established and well known, competition reduces them to the level of other trades.
Second, this equality in the whole of the advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock can hold only in their ordinary, or what we may call their natural, state.

The demand for almost every kind of labour is sometimes greater and sometimes less than usual. In the first case the advantages of the employment rise above the common level, in the second they fall below it. The demand for country labour is greater at haymaking and harvest than during most of the year, and wages rise with the demand. In wartime, when forty or fifty thousand sailors are forced out of the merchant service into the king's, the demand for sailors on merchant ships necessarily rises with their scarcity, and on such occasions their wages commonly rise from a guinea and twenty-seven shillings to forty shillings and three pounds a month. In a declining manufacture, by contrast, many workmen would rather accept lower wages than would otherwise suit the nature of their work than abandon their trade.

The profits of stock vary with the price of the goods in which it is employed. As the price of any commodity rises above its ordinary or average rate, the profits on at least part of the stock employed in bringing it to market rise above their proper level, and as the price falls they sink below it. All commodities are more or less liable to price variations, but some far more than others. In all commodities produced by human industry, the quantity of industry employed each year is necessarily regulated by the yearly demand, so that the average yearly output may come as close as possible to equalling the average yearly consumption. In some employments, as already noted, the same quantity of industry will always produce the same, or very nearly the same, quantity of goods. In the linen or woollen manufactures, for example, the same number of hands will work up very nearly the same quantity of linen and woollen cloth each year, so variations in the market price of such goods can arise only from some accidental variation in demand. A public mourning raises the price of black cloth; but since the demand for most kinds of plain linen and woollen cloth is fairly uniform, so too is the price. There are other employments, however, in which the same quantity of industry will not always produce the same quantity of goods. The same quantity of industry, for example, will in different years produce very different quantities of corn, wine, hops, sugar, tobacco, and the like. The price of such goods, therefore, varies not only with changes in demand but with the much greater and more frequent changes in quantity, and so it fluctuates wildly; and the profit of some of the dealers must necessarily fluctuate with the price of the goods. The operations of the speculative merchant are chiefly directed at such goods: he tries to buy them up when he foresees that their price is likely to rise, and to sell them when it is likely to fall.

Third, this equality in the whole of the advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock can hold only in those that are the sole or principal employments of those who occupy them.

When a person earns his living from one employment that does not take up most of his time, he is often willing to work at another during his spare hours for lower wages than would otherwise suit the nature of that work.

In many parts of Scotland there still exists a class of people called cottars or cottagers, though they were more common some years ago than they are now. They are a kind of outdoor servants to the landlords and farmers. The usual reward they receive from their master is a house, a small garden for pot-herbs, as much grass as will feed a cow, and perhaps an acre or two of poor arable land. When their master needs their labour, he gives them, in addition, two pecks of oatmeal a week, worth about sixteen pence sterling. For much of the year he has little or no need of their labour, and cultivating their own little holding does not fill the time left at their disposal. When such tenants were more numerous than they are now, they are said to have been willing to give their spare time to anyone for a very small reward, and to have worked for lower wages than other labourers. In ancient times they seem to have been common all over Europe. In countries poorly cultivated and worse populated, most landlords and farmers could not otherwise obtain the extra hands that country labour requires at certain seasons. The daily or weekly reward such labourers occasionally received from their masters was clearly not the whole price of their labour; their small holding made up a considerable part of it. Yet this daily or weekly reward has been treated as the whole of it by many writers who have collected the prices of labour and provisions in ancient times and taken pleasure in portraying both as astonishingly low.

The product of such labour often reaches the market more cheaply than its nature would otherwise allow. In many parts of Scotland stockings are knitted far more cheaply than they can anywhere be made on the loom, because they are the work of servants and labourers who draw most of their subsistence from some other employment. More than a thousand pairs of Shetland stockings are imported into Leith each year, at a price of fivepence to sevenpence a pair. At Lerwick, the small capital of the Shetland islands, tenpence a day, I have been assured, is a common price for common labour; and in those same islands they knit worsted stockings worth a guinea a pair and upwards.

The spinning of linen yarn is carried on in Scotland in much the same way as the knitting of stockings, by servants hired chiefly for other purposes. Those who try to make a living by either of these trades earn only a very scanty subsistence. In most parts of Scotland a good spinner is one who can earn twentypence a week.

In wealthy countries the market is generally so large that any single trade is enough to employ the whole labour and stock of those who practise it. Cases of people living by one employment while drawing some small advantage from another occur chiefly in poor countries. The following instance of something of the same kind, however, is to be found in the capital of a very rich one. There is no city in Europe, I believe, where house-rent is dearer than in London, yet I know of no capital where a furnished apartment can be hired so cheaply. Lodging is not only much cheaper in London than in Paris; it is much cheaper than in Edinburgh for the same quality. And, strangely enough, the high cost of house-rent is the cause of the cheapness of lodging. The high cost of house-rent in London arises partly from the causes that make it dear in all great capitals, the high price of labour, the high price of all building materials, which must generally be brought from a great distance, and above all the high price of ground-rent, since every landlord acts as a monopolist and often charges more for a single acre of poor land in a town than could be had for a hundred acres of the best land in the country; but it also arises partly from the particular manners and customs of the people, which oblige every head of a family to rent a whole house from top to bottom. A dwelling-house in England means everything contained under the same roof, whereas in France, Scotland, and many other parts of Europe it often means no more than a single storey. A tradesman in London is obliged to rent a whole house in the part of town where his customers live. His shop is on the ground floor, while he and his family sleep in the garret, and he tries to pay part of his rent by letting the two middle storeys to lodgers. He expects to support his family by his trade, not by his lodgers, whereas in Paris and Edinburgh people who let lodgings commonly have no other means of subsistence, so the price of the lodging must cover not only the rent of the house but the whole expense of the family.
Part II: Inequalities caused by the Policy of Europe.

Such are the inequalities in the whole of the advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock that must arise from the absence of any of the three requisites mentioned above, even where there is the most perfect liberty. But the policy of Europe, by not leaving things at perfect liberty, causes other inequalities of far greater importance.

It does this chiefly in the three following ways. First, by restricting the competition in some employments to fewer people than would otherwise be willing to enter them. Second, by increasing it in others beyond what it would naturally be. And third, by obstructing the free movement of labour and stock, both from one employment to another and from one place to another.

First, the policy of Europe causes a very important inequality in the whole of the advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock by restricting the competition in some employments to fewer people than might otherwise be willing to enter them.
The exclusive privileges granted to corporations are the main tool Europe uses to bring this about.

When a trade is incorporated and given an exclusive privilege, it automatically limits competition within the town to those who are free of the trade. To win that freedom, you normally have to serve an apprenticeship in the town under a master who is properly qualified. The corporation's bye-laws sometimes cap the number of apprentices any one master may take, and they almost always fix the number of years each apprentice must serve. Both rules aim at the same thing: to keep competition far smaller than the number of people who would otherwise want to enter the trade. Capping the number of apprentices limits it directly. A long apprenticeship limits it more indirectly, but just as effectively, by driving up the cost of training.

In Sheffield, a corporation bye-law forbids any master cutler from keeping more than one apprentice at a time. In Norfolk and Norwich, no master weaver may keep more than two apprentices, on pain of forfeiting five pounds a month to the king. No master hatter anywhere in England, or in the English plantations, may keep more than two apprentices, on pain of forfeiting five pounds a month, half to the king and half to whoever sues for it in a court of record. Both of these rules, though they have been confirmed by a public law of the kingdom, are plainly driven by the same corporation spirit that produced the Sheffield bye-law. The silk-weavers in London had barely been incorporated for a year before they passed a bye-law forbidding any master from keeping more than two apprentices at a time. It took a special act of parliament to repeal it.

All across Europe, seven years seems to have been the standard length of apprenticeship in most incorporated trades in earlier times. All such incorporations used to be called universities, which is in fact simply the Latin word for any incorporated body. The university of smiths, the university of tailors, and similar phrases turn up regularly in the old charters of ancient towns. When the particular incorporations we now specifically call universities were first founded, the number of years required to earn the degree of master of arts was plainly copied from the apprenticeship term in ordinary trades, whose incorporations were much older. Just as you had to work seven years under a properly qualified master before you could become a master yourself and take on apprentices in an ordinary trade, so you had to study seven years under a properly qualified master before you could become a master, teacher, or doctor (words that were once interchangeable) in the liberal arts, and take on scholars or apprentices (words that were also originally the same) to study under you.

Under the fifth year of Elizabeth's reign, in the law commonly called the Statute of Apprenticeship, it was enacted that from then on no one could practise any trade, craft, or skilled occupation then carried on in England unless he had first served an apprenticeship of at least seven years to it. What had previously been the bye-law of many individual corporations now became, in England, the general public law of every trade carried on in market towns. The words of the statute are very broad and seem clearly to cover the whole kingdom, but through legal interpretation its scope has been confined to market towns. The courts have held that in country villages a person may carry on several different trades without having served a seven-year apprenticeship to each, since those trades are needed for the convenience of the inhabitants and there are often too few people to supply each trade with its own set of hands. By a strict reading of the words, the statute has also been confined to trades already established in England before the fifth year of Elizabeth, and has never been extended to trades introduced since. This limit has produced several distinctions that, judged as rules of policy, are about as silly as anything could be. The courts have ruled, for instance, that a coach-maker may neither make his own coach-wheels nor employ journeymen to make them, but must buy them from a master wheelwright, because wheelwrighting was practised in England before the fifth year of Elizabeth. Yet a wheelwright, though he has never served an apprenticeship to a coach-maker, may make coaches himself or employ journeymen to make them, because coach-making does not fall under the statute, not having been practised in England when the statute was passed. Many of the manufactures of Manchester, Birmingham, and Wolverhampton fall outside the statute on the same grounds, since they were not practised in England before the fifth year of Elizabeth.

In France, the length of apprenticeship varies from town to town and from trade to trade. In Paris, five years is the term required in a great many trades; but in many of them, before anyone can qualify to practise the trade as a master, he must serve a further five years as a journeyman. During this second stretch he is called his master's companion, and the term itself is called his companionship.

In Scotland there is no general law that sets a uniform length for apprenticeships. The term varies from one corporation to another. Where it is long, part of it can usually be bought off by paying a small fine. In most towns, too, a very small fine is enough to buy the freedom of any corporation. The weavers of linen and hempen cloth, the country's main manufactures, along with all the other craftsmen who support them, such as wheel-makers and reel-makers, may practise their trades in any incorporated town without paying any fine. In every incorporated town, anyone is free to sell butcher's meat on any lawful day of the week. Three years is a common apprenticeship term in Scotland, even in some quite delicate trades, and overall I know of no country in Europe where corporation laws are so little oppressive.

The property each man has in his own labour is the original foundation of all other property, and it is also the most sacred and inviolable. A poor man's inheritance lies in the strength and skill of his hands, and to stop him from using that strength and skill however he sees fit, so long as he harms no neighbour, is a plain violation of this most sacred property. It is an obvious encroachment on the just liberty both of the workman and of anyone who might want to employ him. Just as it stops the one from working at what he chooses, it stops the others from employing whom they choose. Whether a man is fit to be employed can surely be left to the judgement of the employers, whose own interest is so closely involved. The lawmaker's affected concern that they might employ the wrong person is as meddlesome as it is oppressive.

Long apprenticeships are no guarantee that shoddy workmanship will not often be put up for public sale. When that happens, it is usually the result of fraud, not of incompetence, and the longest apprenticeship is no guard against fraud. Preventing that abuse calls for quite different regulations. The sterling mark on silver plate and the stamps on linen and woollen cloth give the buyer far more security than any apprenticeship statute. He normally checks these marks, but never thinks it worth asking whether the workman served a seven-year apprenticeship.

Long apprenticeships do nothing to make young people industrious. A journeyman paid by the piece is likely to work hard, because he gains from every bit of effort. An apprentice is likely to be idle, and almost always is, because he has no immediate stake in being otherwise. In the lower occupations, the rewards of labour consist entirely in the pay for it. Those who are soonest in a position to enjoy that pay are likely to develop a taste for work soonest, and to pick up the habit of industry early. A young man naturally comes to hate work when he gets nothing from it for a long stretch. The boys sent out as apprentices by public charities are usually bound for more than the usual number of years, and they usually turn out very idle and worthless.

Apprenticeships were entirely unknown to the ancients. The mutual duties of master and apprentice make up a substantial part of every modern legal code, yet Roman law says nothing at all about them. I know of no Greek or Latin word, and I think I can safely say there is none, that captures what we now mean by apprentice: a servant bound to work at a particular trade for a master's benefit, over a term of years, on the condition that the master teach him that trade.

Long apprenticeships are entirely unnecessary. The skilled crafts that stand well above ordinary trades, such as making clocks and watches, hold no mystery deep enough to require a long course of instruction. The original invention of such beautiful machines, and even of some of the tools used to make them, must of course have taken deep thought and long time, and rightly ranks among the finest achievements of human ingenuity. But once both have been properly invented and are well understood, explaining to any young man, in the fullest possible way, how to use the tools and how to build the machines need not take more than a few weeks of lessons; perhaps a few days would do. In the ordinary mechanical trades a few days would certainly be enough. Manual dexterity, even in ordinary trades, cannot be acquired without a great deal of practice and experience. But a young man would practise with far more diligence and care if from the start he worked as a journeyman, paid in proportion to the little he could produce, and paying in turn for the materials he might spoil now and then through clumsiness and inexperience. His training would generally be more effective this way, and always less tedious and less expensive. The master, it is true, would lose out. He would lose all the apprentice's wages that he now saves over seven years together. In the end the apprentice himself might lose out too. In a trade so easily learnt he would face more competitors, and his wages, once he became a finished workman, would be much lower than they are now. The same rise in competition would cut the masters' profits as well as the workmen's wages. The trades, the crafts, the skilled occupations would all be losers. But the public would gain, because the work of all these craftsmen would reach the market far cheaper.

It is to prevent this fall in price, and so in wages and profit, by suppressing the free competition that would certainly cause it, that all corporations and most corporation laws have been set up. In earlier times, in many parts of Europe, no authority was needed to create a corporation except that of the incorporated town where it was established. In England, admittedly, a charter from the king was also required. But this royal prerogative seems to have been kept up more as a way of squeezing money out of subjects than as a defence of common liberty against such oppressive monopolies. On payment of a fine to the king, the charter was generally granted readily enough; and when a particular group of craftsmen or traders chose to act as a corporation without a charter, such bodies, called adulterine guilds, were not always stripped of their privileges on that account, but were merely required to pay the king an annual fine for permission to exercise their usurped rights (see Madox, Firma Burgi, p. 26 and following). Direct oversight of all corporations, and of any bye-laws they chose to enact for their own governance, belonged to the incorporated town where they were based; and whatever discipline was applied to them came, as a rule, not from the king, but from that larger incorporated body of which these lesser ones were only parts or members.

The government of incorporated towns lay entirely in the hands of traders and craftsmen, and it was plainly in the interest of each particular group of them to keep the market from being overstocked, as they usually put it, with its own kind of work, which really means keeping it permanently understocked. Each group was eager to set up regulations to serve this purpose and, provided it was allowed to do so, was happy to let every other group do the same. As a result of such regulations, each group did have to buy the goods it needed from every other group in the town at somewhat higher prices than it might otherwise have paid. But in return it could sell its own goods at correspondingly higher prices; so on that score it came out about even, as the saying goes, and in their dealings with one another none of the different groups within the town lost anything by these regulations. In their dealings with the countryside, however, they all gained greatly, and it is in these latter dealings that the whole trade which supports and enriches every town consists.

Every town draws its entire subsistence, and all the raw materials for its industry, from the countryside. It pays for these mainly in two ways. First, by sending part of those materials back to the country worked up and manufactured; in which case their price is raised by the wages of the workmen and the profits of their masters or direct employers. Second, by sending the country a portion of the raw and manufactured produce of other countries, or of distant parts of the same country, that has been imported into the town; in which case the original price of those goods is likewise raised by the wages of the carriers or sailors and by the profits of the merchants who employ them. The gain on the first of these branches of commerce is the advantage the town makes from its manufactures; the gain on the second is the advantage of its inland and foreign trade. The wages of the workmen and the profits of their various employers make up the whole of what is gained on both. Any regulation, therefore, that raises those wages and profits above what they would otherwise be lets the town buy the produce of a greater quantity of country labour with a smaller quantity of its own. It gives the traders and craftsmen of the town an advantage over the landlords, farmers, and labourers of the country, and destroys the natural equality that would otherwise hold in the commerce carried on between them. The whole annual produce of the society's labour is divided each year between these two different sets of people. By means of such regulations, a larger share of it goes to the townspeople than would otherwise fall to them, and a smaller share to the country.

The price a town really pays for the provisions and materials imported into it each year is the quantity of manufactures and other goods it exports each year. The dearer it sells the latter, the cheaper it buys the former. The town's industry becomes more advantageous, the country's less so.

We do not need fine calculations to convince ourselves that town industry is everywhere in Europe more advantageous than country industry; one simple, obvious observation will do. In every European country we find at least a hundred people who have made great fortunes from small beginnings through trade and manufactures, the industry that properly belongs to towns, for every one who has done so through the industry that properly belongs to the country, the raising of raw produce by improving and cultivating land. Industry must therefore be better rewarded, and the wages of labour and the profits of stock must clearly be higher, in the one setting than in the other. But stock and labour naturally seek out the most advantageous employment. They therefore flock as much as they can to the town and abandon the country.

Because townspeople are gathered together in one place, they can easily combine. So even the most trivial trades carried on in towns have, somewhere or other, been incorporated; and even where they never have been, the corporation spirit, the suspicion of outsiders, the reluctance to take apprentices or to share the secrets of the trade, generally prevails, and often teaches them, through voluntary associations and agreements, to block the free competition they cannot forbid by bye-law. The trades that employ only a few hands slide most easily into such combinations. Perhaps half a dozen wool-combers are needed to keep a thousand spinners and weavers at work. By agreeing not to take apprentices, they can not only monopolise the work but reduce the whole manufacture to a kind of slavery under them, and push the price of their labour far above what the nature of their work warrants.

Country people, scattered across distant places, cannot easily combine. Not only have they never been incorporated, but the corporation spirit has never taken hold among them. No apprenticeship has ever been thought necessary to qualify a man for farming, the great trade of the country. Yet apart from what are called the fine arts and the liberal professions, there is perhaps no trade that demands so great a variety of knowledge and experience. The countless volumes written on it in every language may convince us that even among the wisest and most learned nations it has never been seen as a thing easily understood. And from all those volumes we shall try in vain to extract the knowledge of its many complicated operations that even the ordinary farmer commonly possesses, however contemptuously the very contemptible authors of some of them may sometimes speak of him. By contrast, there is hardly any common mechanical trade whose every operation cannot be explained as fully and clearly as words and diagrams allow in a pamphlet of just a few pages. In the history of the arts now being published by the French Academy of Sciences, several of them are in fact explained in exactly this way. What is more, directing operations that must be adjusted with every change in the weather, and with many other accidents besides, calls for far more judgement and discretion than directing operations that are always, or very nearly, the same.

Not only the farmer's art, the general direction of farming operations, but many lesser branches of country labour demand far more skill and experience than most mechanical trades. The man who works in brass and iron works with tools, and on materials, whose temper is always the same, or nearly so. But the man who ploughs the ground with a team of horses or oxen works with tools whose health, strength, and temper vary greatly from one occasion to the next. The condition of the materials he works on is as variable as that of the tools he works with, and both must be handled with much judgement and discretion. The common ploughman, though generally taken as the very model of stupidity and ignorance, is seldom lacking in this judgement and discretion. He is less used to social company, it is true, than the mechanic who lives in a town. His voice and speech are rougher and harder to follow for those not used to them. But his understanding, accustomed to weighing a greater variety of objects, is generally much superior to that of the townsman, whose whole attention from morning to night is usually taken up with one or two very simple operations. Anyone whom business or curiosity has led to talk much with both knows well how far the lower ranks of country people really surpass those of the town. In China and Hindustan, accordingly, both the standing and the wages of country labourers are said to be higher than those of most craftsmen and manufacturers. They would probably be so everywhere if corporation laws and the corporation spirit did not prevent it.

The advantage that town industry enjoys everywhere in Europe over country industry is not entirely due to corporations and corporation laws. It is propped up by many other regulations too. The heavy duties on foreign manufactures, and on all goods imported by foreign merchants, all serve the same end. Corporation laws let townspeople raise their prices without fear of being undersold by the free competition of their own countrymen. Those other regulations protect them just as well against the competition of foreigners. The price increase caused by both is in the end always paid by the landlords, farmers, and labourers of the country, who have seldom opposed the setting up of such monopolies. They usually have neither the inclination nor the aptitude to form combinations; and the noise and clever arguments of merchants and manufacturers easily persuade them that the private interest of one part of society, and a subordinate part at that, is the general interest of the whole.

In Great Britain, town industry seems to have held a greater advantage over country industry in former times than it does now. The wages of country labour come nearer to those of manufacturing labour, and the profits of stock employed in farming nearer to those of stock employed in trade and manufacture, than they are said to have done in the last century or at the start of the present one. This change may be seen as the necessary, though very late, consequence of the extraordinary encouragement given to town industry. The stocks built up in towns grow so large in time that they can no longer be employed at the old profit in the kind of industry peculiar to towns. That industry, like every other, has its limits; and as stock grows, the increased competition necessarily drives down profit. The fall in town profit pushes stock out into the country, where, by creating fresh demand for country labour, it necessarily raises country wages. The stock then spreads, if I may put it so, over the face of the land, and, by being employed in farming, is partly returned to the country at whose expense it had largely been built up in the town in the first place. I shall try later to show that everywhere in Europe the greatest improvements of the countryside have come from such overflowings of stock originally accumulated in the towns, and at the same time to show that although some countries have by this route reached a considerable degree of wealth, the process is necessarily slow, uncertain, easily disturbed and interrupted by countless accidents, and in every respect contrary to the order of nature and of reason. The interests, prejudices, laws, and customs that have given rise to it I shall try to explain as fully and clearly as I can in the third and fourth books of this inquiry.

People in the same trade seldom meet together, even for fun and recreation, without the conversation ending in a conspiracy against the public, or in some scheme to raise prices. It is impossible, of course, to prevent such meetings by any law that could either be enforced or be consistent with liberty and justice. But although the law cannot stop people in the same trade from gathering now and then, it should do nothing to make such gatherings easier, still less to make them necessary.

A regulation that requires everyone in the same trade in a particular town to register their names and addresses in a public record makes such gatherings easier. It links up individuals who might otherwise never have known each other, and tells every man in the trade where to find every other.

A regulation that lets people in the same trade tax themselves in order to provide for their poor, their sick, their widows and orphans, gives them a common interest to manage and so makes such gatherings necessary.

Incorporation not only makes such gatherings necessary but makes the decision of the majority binding on everyone. In a free trade, an effective combination can be set up only by the unanimous agreement of every single trader, and it can last only as long as every single trader stays of the same mind. The majority of a corporation, by contrast, can pass a bye-law with proper penalties that will limit competition more effectively and more lastingly than any voluntary combination ever could.

The claim that corporations are needed for the better governance of a trade has no foundation. The real and effective discipline a workman is subject to comes not from his corporation but from his customers. It is the fear of losing their custom that checks his frauds and corrects his carelessness. An exclusive corporation necessarily weakens this discipline. A fixed set of workmen then has to be employed, whether they behave well or badly. That is why, in many large incorporated towns, no decent workmen can be found even in some of the most essential trades. If you want your work done at all well, it has to be done in the suburbs, where the workmen, having no exclusive privilege, have nothing to rely on but their reputation, and then you must smuggle it into the town as best you can.

It is in this way that the policy of Europe, by restricting competition in certain occupations to fewer people than would otherwise want to enter them, creates a very significant inequality across the whole range of advantages and disadvantages in the different employments of labour and stock.

Secondly, the policy of Europe, by raising competition in certain occupations above its natural level, creates another inequality, of the opposite kind, across the whole range of advantages and disadvantages in the different employments of labour and stock.

It has been thought so important that a proper number of young people be trained for certain professions that sometimes the state, and sometimes the piety of private founders, has set up many pensions, scholarships, exhibitions, bursaries, and the like for the purpose, which draw far more people into those professions than could otherwise hope to follow them. In every Christian country, I believe, the education of most clergymen is paid for in this way. Very few of them are educated entirely at their own expense. So the long, tedious, and expensive education of those who are will not always earn them a fitting reward, since the church is crowded with people who, in order to get a post, are willing to accept a much smaller payment than their education would otherwise have entitled them to; and in this way the competition of the poor strips the rich of their reward. It would be improper, no doubt, to compare a curate or a chaplain with a journeyman in any ordinary trade. Yet the pay of a curate or chaplain may fairly be regarded as the same in nature as a journeyman's wages. All three are paid for their work according to whatever contract they happen to make with their respective superiors. Until after the middle of the fourteenth century, five marks, containing about as much silver as ten pounds of our present money, was the usual pay in England for a curate or a stipendiary parish priest, as we find it fixed by the decrees of several different national councils. In the same period, fourpence a day, containing the same quantity of silver as a shilling of our present money, was declared to be the pay of a master mason, and threepence a day, equal to ninepence of our present money, that of a journeyman mason (see the Statute of Labourers, 25 Edward III). The wages of both these labourers, then, assuming they were kept constantly employed, were much higher than the curate's. Even if the master mason had been out of work a third of the year, his wages would still have fully matched the curate's. By the twelfth year of Queen Anne, chapter 12, it is declared that "whereas, for want of sufficient maintenance and encouragement to curates, the cures have, in several places, been meanly supplied, the bishop is, therefore, empowered to appoint, by writing under his hand and seal, a sufficient certain stipend or allowance, not exceeding fifty, and not less than twenty pounds a-year." Forty pounds a year is now reckoned very good pay for a curate; and despite this act of parliament, there are many curacies worth less than twenty pounds a year. There are journeyman shoemakers in London who earn forty pounds a year, and there is hardly a hard-working tradesman of any kind in that city who does not earn more than twenty. That last figure, indeed, is no more than what common labourers often earn in many country parishes. Whenever the law has tried to regulate workmen's wages, it has always been to lower them rather than to raise them. But on many occasions the law has tried to raise curates' wages, and, for the dignity of the church, to force parish rectors to pay them more than the wretched maintenance the curates themselves would be willing to take. In both cases the law has proved equally useless, and has never managed either to raise curates' wages or to push labourers' wages down to the intended level; because it has never been able to stop the curate from being willing to take less than the legal allowance, given the poverty of his situation and the throng of his competitors, or to stop the labourer from getting more, given the opposing competition of those who hoped to gain either profit or pleasure from employing him.

The great benefices and other church dignities uphold the honour of the church, despite the meagre circumstances of some of its lower members. The respect paid to the profession also makes some amends, even to them, for the poverty of their pay. In England, and in all Roman Catholic countries, the lottery of the church is in fact far more rewarding than it needs to be. The example of the churches of Scotland, of Geneva, and of several other Protestant churches may convince us that in so respectable a profession, where education is so easily obtained, the prospect of much more modest benefices will draw enough learned, decent, and respectable men into holy orders.

In professions that have no benefices, such as law and medicine, if an equal proportion of people were educated at public expense, competition would soon grow so fierce as to drive their pay right down. It might then not be worth any man's while to pay for his son's training in either profession out of his own pocket. They would be left entirely to those educated by such public charities, whose numbers and poverty would generally force them to settle for a very miserable reward, completely degrading the now respectable professions of law and medicine.

That luckless breed of men commonly called men of letters are pretty much in the position lawyers and physicians would be in under the supposition just made. In every part of Europe, most of them were educated for the church, but were kept from entering holy orders for one reason or another. They have therefore generally been educated at public expense; and their numbers are everywhere so great as commonly to drive the price of their labour down to a very paltry reward.

Before the invention of printing, the only way a man of letters could earn anything by his talents was as a public or private teacher, by passing on to others the curious and useful knowledge he had gained himself; and this is surely still a more honourable, a more useful, and generally even a more profitable occupation than the other one printing has given rise to, writing for a bookseller. The time and study, the genius, knowledge, and application needed to make an eminent teacher of the sciences are at least equal to what the greatest practitioners of law and medicine require. But the usual reward of the eminent teacher bears no comparison to that of the lawyer or physician, because the teacher's profession is crowded with poor people who were brought up to it at public expense, whereas the other two are burdened with very few who were not educated at their own. Even the usual pay of public and private teachers, small as it may seem, would no doubt be smaller still if the competition of those still more destitute men of letters who write for a living were not kept out of the market. Before printing was invented, a scholar and a beggar seem to have been almost interchangeable terms. The various heads of universities, before that time, appear often to have granted their scholars licences to beg.

In ancient times, before any charities of this kind had been set up to educate poor people for the learned professions, the rewards of eminent teachers appear to have been far greater. Isocrates, in what is called his discourse against the sophists, reproaches the teachers of his own day with inconsistency. "They make the most magnificent promises to their scholars," he says, "and undertake to teach them to be wise, to be happy, and to be just; and, in return for so important a service, they stipulate the paltry reward of four or five minae." "Those who teach wisdom," he goes on, "ought certainly to be wise themselves; but if any man were to sell such a bargain for such a price, he would be convicted of the most evident folly." He certainly does not mean here to overstate the reward, and we may be sure it was no less than he says. Four minae came to thirteen pounds six shillings and eightpence; five minae to sixteen pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence. So something not less than the larger of those two sums must at that time have been the usual pay of the most eminent teachers at Athens. Isocrates himself charged ten minae, or 33 pounds 6 shillings 8 pence, from each scholar. When he taught at Athens he is said to have had a hundred scholars. I take this to be the number he taught at one time, or who attended what we would call one course of lectures; a number that will not seem extraordinary for so great a city and so famous a teacher, who taught, what is more, what was then the most fashionable of all subjects, rhetoric. He must therefore have made, from each course of lectures, a thousand minae, or 3,335 pounds 6 shillings 8 pence. A thousand minae is in fact named by Plutarch, in another passage, as his didactron, or usual fee for teaching. Many other eminent teachers of those times appear to have amassed great fortunes. Gorgias made a present to the temple of Delphi of a statue of himself in solid gold. We must not, I suppose, imagine it was life-size. His manner of living, like that of Hippias and Protagoras, two other eminent teachers of the time, is portrayed by Plato as splendid, even to the point of ostentation. Plato himself is said to have lived with a good deal of magnificence. Aristotle, after serving as tutor to Alexander, and being most generously rewarded, as everyone agrees, by both him and his father Philip, still thought it worth his while to return to Athens to take up teaching at his school again. Teachers of the sciences were probably less common in those days than they became an age or two later, when competition had probably somewhat reduced both the price of their labour and the admiration for their persons. Yet the most eminent of them seem always to have enjoyed a standing far above any of their profession today.
