The Athenians sent Carneades the Academic and Diogenes the Stoic on a solemn embassy to Rome; and although their city had by then declined from its former greatness, it was still an independent and considerable republic.

Carneades, moreover, was a Babylonian by birth; and since no people was ever more reluctant to admit foreigners to public office than the Athenians, the regard they showed him must have been very great.

On the whole, this inequality is perhaps more beneficial than harmful to the public. It may somewhat lower the standing of the public teacher; but the cheapness of education is surely an advantage that far outweighs this small drawback. The public might draw even greater benefit from it if the constitution of the schools and colleges where education is carried on were more sensible than it is at present across most of Europe.

Thirdly, the policy of Europe, by blocking the free movement of labour and stock, both from one employment to another and from one place to another, creates in some cases a very awkward inequality across the whole range of advantages and disadvantages in their different employments.

The Statute of Apprenticeship blocks the free movement of labour from one employment to another, even within the same place. The exclusive privileges of corporations block its movement from one place to another, even within the same employment.

It often happens that while high wages are paid to the workmen in one manufacture, those in another must make do with bare subsistence. The first is in a rising state and so has a constant demand for new hands; the second is in decline, and its surplus of hands keeps growing. These two manufactures may sometimes be in the same town, sometimes even in the same neighbourhood, without being able to give one another the least relief. The Statute of Apprenticeship may bar it in the one case, and both that and an exclusive corporation in the other. Yet in many different manufactures the operations are so alike that the workmen could easily switch trades with one another, if those absurd laws did not stop them. The crafts of weaving plain linen and plain silk, for instance, are almost identical. Weaving plain woollen is somewhat different, but the difference is so slight that either a linen or a silk weaver could become a passable workman in a very few days. So if any of those three major manufactures were declining, the workmen could fall back on whichever of the other two was in a more flourishing state; and their wages would neither rise too high in the thriving trade nor sink too low in the failing one. The linen manufacture, it is true, is open to everyone in England by a particular statute; but since it is not much pursued through most of the country, it offers no general refuge to the workmen of other declining manufactures, who, wherever the Statute of Apprenticeship applies, have no choice but to fall on the parish or work as common labourers, for which their habits make them far less suited than for any manufacture resembling their own. So they generally choose to fall on the parish.

Whatever blocks the free movement of labour from one employment to another blocks that of stock as well, since the quantity of stock that can be used in any branch of business depends very much on the quantity of labour that can be used in it. Corporation laws, however, hinder the free movement of stock from place to place less than they hinder that of labour. Everywhere it is much easier for a wealthy merchant to obtain the right to trade in an incorporated town than for a poor craftsman to obtain the right to work in it.

The hindrance that corporation laws place on the free movement of labour is common, I believe, to every part of Europe. The hindrance placed on it by the poor laws is, as far as I know, peculiar to England. It lies in the difficulty a poor man finds in gaining a settlement, or even in being allowed to practise his trade in any parish but the one he belongs to. Corporation laws obstruct the free movement only of craftsmen and manufacturers. The difficulty of gaining settlements obstructs even that of common labour. It may be worth giving some account of the rise, progress, and present state of this disorder, perhaps the greatest of any in the policing of England.

When the destruction of the monasteries deprived the poor of the charity of those religious houses, and after some other ineffective attempts to relieve them, it was enacted, by the forty-third year of Elizabeth, chapter 2, that every parish should be obliged to provide for its own poor, and that overseers of the poor should be appointed each year who, together with the churchwardens, should raise adequate sums for the purpose through a parish rate.

By this statute, the duty of providing for their own poor was firmly imposed on every parish. Who counted as the poor of each parish therefore became a question of some importance. After some variation, this question was finally settled by the thirteenth and fourteenth years of Charles II, when it was enacted that forty days of undisturbed residence should gain anyone a settlement in any parish; but that within that time, on a complaint by the churchwardens or overseers of the poor, two justices of the peace could remove any new resident to the parish where he was last legally settled, unless he either rented a property worth ten pounds a year or could give such security against any charge to the parish where he was then living as the justices judged sufficient.

Some frauds, it is said, followed from this statute, parish officers sometimes bribing their own poor to slip off quietly to another parish and, by keeping out of sight for forty days, gain a settlement there, relieving the parish they really belonged to. So it was enacted, by the first year of James II, that the forty days of undisturbed residence needed to gain a settlement should be counted only from the time a person gave written notice, to one of the churchwardens or overseers of the parish he came to live in, of his address and the size of his family.

But parish officers, it seems, were not always more honest about their own poor than they had been about those of other parishes, and sometimes turned a blind eye to such intrusions, accepting the notice and then taking no proper steps in response. Since every person in a parish was supposed to have an interest in preventing as far as possible their being burdened by such intruders, it was further enacted, by the third year of William III, that the forty days of residence should be counted only from the reading out of such written notice in church on a Sunday, immediately after divine service.

"After all," says Doctor Burn, "this kind of settlement, by continuing forty days after publication of notice in writing, is very seldom obtained; and the design of the acts is not so much for gaining of settlements, as for the avoiding of them by persons coming into a parish clandestinely, for the giving of notice is only putting a force upon the parish to remove. But if a person's situation is such, that it is doubtful whether he is actually removable or not, he shall, by giving of notice, compel the parish either to allow him a settlement uncontested, by suffering him to continue forty days, or by removing him to try the right."

This statute, then, made it almost impossible for a poor man to gain a new settlement the old way, by forty days of residence. But so as not to seem to shut off the common people of one parish from ever settling securely in another, it laid down four other ways a settlement might be gained without any notice given or published. The first was by being assessed for parish rates and paying them; the second, by being elected to an annual parish office and serving in it for a year; the third, by serving an apprenticeship in the parish; the fourth, by being hired into service there for a year and staying in the same service throughout it. No one can gain a settlement by either of the first two ways except by the public act of the whole parish, who know the consequences too well to take on any newcomer with nothing but his labour to support him, whether by assessing him for parish rates or by electing him to a parish office.

No married man can well gain a settlement by either of the last two ways. An apprentice is hardly ever married; and it is expressly enacted that no married servant shall gain a settlement by being hired for a year. The main effect of introducing settlement by service has been largely to do away with the old custom of hiring for a year, which had once been so usual in England that even now, if no particular term is agreed, the law assumes every servant is hired for a year. But masters are not always willing to give their servants a settlement by hiring them this way; and servants are not always willing to be hired this way, because, since every new settlement cancels all earlier ones, they might thereby lose their original settlement in their birthplace, the home of their parents and relations.

Clearly no independent workman, whether labourer or craftsman, is likely to gain a new settlement either by apprenticeship or by service. So when such a man took his trade to a new parish, he was liable to be removed, however healthy and hard-working he might be, at the whim of any churchwarden or overseer, unless he either rented a property worth ten pounds a year, an impossibility for someone with nothing but his labour to live on, or could give such security against any charge to the parish as two justices of the peace judged sufficient.

What security they may demand is, in fact, left entirely to their discretion; but they can hardly demand less than thirty pounds, since it has been enacted that the purchase even of a freehold estate worth less than thirty pounds shall not gain anyone a settlement, as being insufficient to indemnify the parish. But this is a security scarcely any man who lives by labour can give, and far greater security is often demanded.

To restore, in some measure, the free movement of labour that these various statutes had almost entirely taken away, the device of certificates was hit upon. By the eighth and ninth years of William III, it was enacted that if anyone brought a certificate from the parish where he was last legally settled, signed by the churchwardens and overseers of the poor and approved by two justices of the peace, every other parish should be obliged to receive him; that he should not be removable merely on the grounds that he was likely to become a charge, but only once he actually became one; and that the parish which granted the certificate should then be obliged to pay the cost both of his maintenance and of his removal. And to give the fullest possible security to the parish where such a certificated man came to live, the same statute further enacted that he should gain no settlement there by any means whatever, except by renting a property worth ten pounds a year or by serving on his own account in an annual parish office for one whole year; and so neither by notice, nor by service, nor by apprenticeship, nor by paying parish rates. By the twelfth year of Queen Anne, statute 1, chapter 18, it was further enacted that neither the servants nor the apprentices of such a certificated man should gain any settlement in the parish where he lived under such a certificate.

How far this device has restored the free movement of labour that the earlier statutes had almost entirely taken away we may judge from the following very shrewd remark of Doctor Burn. "It is obvious," he says, "that there are divers good reasons for requiring certificates with persons coming to settle in any place; namely, that persons residing under them can gain no settlement, neither by apprenticeship, nor by service, nor by giving notice, nor by paying parish rates; that they can settle neither apprentices nor servants; that if they become chargeable, it is certainly known whither to remove them, and the parish shall be paid for the removal, and for their maintenance in the mean time; and that, if they fall sick, and cannot be removed, the parish which gave the certificate must maintain them; none of all which can be without a certificate. Which reasons will hold proportionably for parishes not granting certificates in ordinary cases; for it is far more than an equal chance, but that they will have the certificated persons again, and in a worse condition." The moral of this observation seems to be that certificates ought always to be required by the parish a poor man comes to live in, and ought very seldom to be granted by the one he means to leave. "There is somewhat of hardship in this matter of certificates," says the same very intelligent author, in his History of the Poor Laws, "by putting it in the power of a parish officer to imprison a man as it were for life, however inconvenient it may be for him to continue at that place where he has had the misfortune to acquire what is called a settlement, or whatever advantage he may propose himself by living elsewhere."

Though a certificate carries no testimony of good behaviour, and certifies nothing but that the person belongs to the parish he really does belong to, it is entirely up to the parish officers whether to grant or refuse it. A mandamus was once moved for, says Doctor Burn, to compel the churchwardens and overseers to sign a certificate; but the Court of King's Bench rejected the motion as a very strange attempt.

The very uneven price of labour we often find in England, in places not far apart, is probably due to the obstruction that the law of settlements puts in the way of a poor man who would carry his trade from one parish to another without a certificate. A single man, if healthy and hard-working, may sometimes be allowed to stay without one; but a man with a wife and family who tried to do so would, in most parishes, be sure of being removed; and if the single man later married, he too would generally be removed. So a shortage of hands in one parish cannot always be relieved by a surplus in another, as it constantly is in Scotland, and, I believe, in every other country where settlement is no difficulty. In such countries, wages may sometimes rise a little near a great town, or wherever else there is an unusual demand for labour, and sink gradually as the distance from such places grows, until they drop back to the country's common rate; but we never meet those sudden, unaccountable differences in the wages of neighbouring places that we sometimes find in England, where it is often harder for a poor man to cross the artificial boundary of a parish than an arm of the sea or a ridge of high mountains, natural boundaries that sometimes mark off very distinctly different rates of wages in other countries.

To remove a man who has committed no offence from the parish where he chooses to live is a plain violation of natural liberty and justice. Yet the common people of England, so jealous of their liberty, but, like the common people of most countries, never quite grasping what it consists in, have now for more than a century allowed themselves to be exposed to this oppression without any remedy. Though thoughtful men have sometimes complained of the law of settlements as a public grievance, it has never become the target of any general popular outcry, like the outcry against general warrants, an abusive practice no doubt, but one not likely to cause any widespread oppression. I will venture to say there is hardly a poor man in England, forty years of age, who has not at some point in his life felt himself most cruelly oppressed by this ill-contrived law of settlements.

I shall close this long chapter by noting that, although in earlier times it was usual to fix wages, first by general laws covering the whole kingdom and later by particular orders of the justices of the peace in each county, both practices have now fallen completely out of use. "By the experience of above four hundred years," says Doctor Burn, "it seems time to lay aside all endeavours to bring under strict regulations, what in its own nature seems incapable of minute limitation; for if all persons in the same kind of work were to receive equal wages, there would be no emulation, and no room left for industry or ingenuity."

Particular acts of parliament, however, still sometimes try to regulate wages in particular trades and particular places. The eighth year of George III, for instance, forbids, under heavy penalties, all master tailors in London and within five miles of it from giving, and their workmen from accepting, more than two shillings and sevenpence halfpenny a day, except in a time of general mourning. Whenever the legislature tries to settle disputes between masters and their workmen, its advisers are always the masters. So when the regulation favours the workmen, it is always fair and equitable; but it is sometimes otherwise when it favours the masters. Thus the law that obliges the masters in several different trades to pay their workmen in money, not in goods, is quite fair and equitable. It imposes no real hardship on the masters. It only obliges them to pay in money the value they pretended to pay, but did not always really pay, in goods. That law favours the workmen; but the eighth of George III favours the masters. When masters combine to cut their workmen's wages, they commonly enter into a private bond or agreement not to give more than a certain wage, under a certain penalty. If the workmen were to enter into an opposite combination of the same kind, not to accept less than a certain wage, under a certain penalty, the law would punish them very severely; and if it dealt fairly, it would treat the masters the same way. But the eighth of George III enforces by law the very regulation that masters sometimes try to set up by such combinations. The workmen's complaint, that it puts the ablest and most industrious on the same footing as an ordinary workman, seems perfectly well founded.

In ancient times, too, it was usual to try to regulate the profits of merchants and other dealers by regulating the price of provisions and other goods. The assize of bread is, as far as I know, the only remnant of this ancient practice. Where there is an exclusive corporation, it may perhaps be proper to regulate the price of the first necessary of life; but where there is none, competition will regulate it far better than any assize. The method of fixing the assize of bread laid down by the thirty-first of George II could not be put into practice in Scotland, because of a defect in the law, its enforcement depending on the office of clerk of the market, which does not exist there. This defect was not remedied until the third of George III. The lack of an assize caused no noticeable inconvenience; and setting one up in the few places where it has so far been done has produced no noticeable benefit. In most of the towns of Scotland, however, there is an incorporation of bakers who claim exclusive privileges, though these are not very strictly guarded. The proportion between the different rates of wages and of profit in the different employments of labour and stock seems not to be much affected, as already noted, by the wealth or poverty, or the advancing, stationary, or declining state, of the society. Such upheavals in the public condition, though they affect the general rates both of wages and of profit, must in the end affect them equally across all the different employments. So the proportion between them must stay the same, and cannot well be altered, at least for any length of time, by any such upheavals.
